entities.summary:
Epistle of Jude

Identity & Significance: The Epistle of Jude, traditionally attributed to Jude, brother of James, is a canonical Christian text in the New Testament of the Bible. Written around 100 CE, it is the shortest book in the New Testament, consisting of 25 verses. The epistle is a response to false teachers and heresy within the early Christian community, warning against the dangers of false doctrine and emphasizing the importance of faith in Jesus Christ. It is considered a significant work in the early Christian canon, offering insight into the theological debates and controversies of the time.

What Happened: The Epistle of Jude recounts the author's personal experience with false teachers who were corrupting the Christian community. The epistle is a call to action, urging believers to remain faithful to the truth of Christ and to reject the false teachings of the heretics. The author also emphasizes the importance of perseverance in the face of persecution and the need for unity among believers.

Legacy & Consequence: The Epistle of Jude has had a lasting impact on Christian theology and practice. It has been widely studied and interpreted throughout history, and its teachings continue to influence Christian thought and culture today. The epistle has also been an important source of inspiration for many Christian leaders and writers, including Martin Luther and John Calvin.

Vivid Closing: 'So I urge you, dear brothers and sisters, to watch out for one another, to look after each other, to love each other, to be kind to one another, and to be humble.' (2 John 1:12).
